questions.stem: A college needs someone to teach physiological psychology and no qualified instructor is available. Dr. Marsh, who knows very little about the field, offers to teach it so the course can run. Under Standards 7.01 through 7.06, this is:

choices.text: unacceptable, since the unavailability of others does not excuse teaching outside one's competence
acceptable, since Standard 2.01(d) permits services where no other qualified provider is available
acceptable, provided he tells students at the outset that the field is new to him
unacceptable only if a student later complains about the quality of the instruction

questions.explanation: Standards 7.01 through 7.06 require psychologists to act competently when teaching and to take reasonable steps not to misrepresent their work. The section gives teaching a physiological psychology class one knows little about, offered because no one else was available, as an example of what these standards forbid.

whyWrong.b: 2.01(d) concerns providing psychological services to a recipient with no alternative provider, not staffing a course.
whyWrong.c: Disclosure does not create competence to teach the material.
whyWrong.d: The violation lies in undertaking the teaching, not in whether a complaint follows.

questions.stem: Dr. Petrov has successfully treated two clients with agoraphobia. He begins advertising himself as an expert on the disorder. This is best described as:

choices.text: acceptable, since he has genuine treatment experience with the disorder
a misrepresentation of his work, contrary to Standards 7.01 through 7.06
acceptable, provided his advertising does not name the two clients
a breach of Standard 5.05, which governs the solicitation of testimonials

questions.explanation: The standards require reasonable steps to avoid misrepresenting oneself or one's work. Claiming expertise on the basis of two successful cases is the section's own example of such a misrepresentation.

whyWrong.a: Some experience is not expertise, and the claim is what makes the conduct a misrepresentation.
whyWrong.c: Client confidentiality is a separate matter and does not cure an inflated claim of expertise.
whyWrong.d: 5.05 concerns testimonials from clients, which is not what is described.

questions.stem: Standards 7.01 through 7.06 are best characterized as:

choices.text: creating obligations that appear nowhere else in the Ethics Code
applying only to psychologists holding full-time academic appointments
restating earlier provisions in the context of education and supervision
supplanting the competence requirements of Standard 2.01 for teaching work

questions.explanation: The section notes these standards largely reiterate earlier provisions but place them within the context of education and supervision — teaching, supervising, and designing training programs.

whyWrong.a: The point is that they restate obligations found elsewhere rather than creating new ones.
whyWrong.b: They reach supervision and program design, not only academic appointments.
whyWrong.d: They apply the competence requirement in this context rather than replacing it.

questions.stem: Six weeks into a semester, Dr. Achebe realizes the assigned final project will not meet the course's learning objectives and wants to replace it. Under Standard 7.03 she may do so if:

choices.text: a majority of the enrolled students vote to accept the proposed change
the syllabus reserved a general right to alter requirements during the term
she cannot: Standard 7.03 requires that syllabi be followed exactly as published
the change is pedagogically warranted and students are told in time to comply

questions.explanation: Standard 7.03 requires accurate syllabi but does not preclude modifying course requirements where the modification is pedagogically necessary or desirable and students are made aware in a timely manner that allows them to complete the new requirements.

whyWrong.a: A student vote is not the condition the standard sets.
whyWrong.b: A reserved right does not satisfy the two conditions the standard actually imposes.
whyWrong.c: This misreads the standard, which expressly permits pedagogically warranted modification.

questions.stem: Standard 7.03 permits modification of course requirements where the change is:

choices.text: pedagogically necessary or desirable
administratively convenient for the department
requested in writing by the students affected
approved in advance by the program's accrediting body

questions.explanation: The standard's phrase is that the modification be pedagogically necessary or desirable, with timely notice to students so they can complete the new requirements.

whyWrong.b: Administrative convenience is not a pedagogical justification.
whyWrong.c: Student request is not the criterion the standard names.
whyWrong.d: No accreditor pre-approval is required for a change of course requirements.

questions.stem: A graduate program requires students to discuss their own family histories in a required group experience. Under Standard 7.04, this requirement is permissible if:

choices.text: each student signs a waiver acknowledging the disclosure requirement at enrolment
it is clearly stated in admissions or other promotional materials
the faculty member leading the group is not involved in grading those students
the disclosures are kept confidential within the group and not recorded

questions.explanation: Standard 7.04 prohibits requiring students or supervisees to disclose personal information unless the requirement is clearly stated in admissions or other promotional materials, or the information is needed to evaluate or assist a student whose personal problems interfere with training or pose a threat to others.

whyWrong.a: A waiver signed at enrolment comes too late; the point is that applicants know before applying.
whyWrong.c: Separating the evaluative role is prudent but is not the exception the standard provides.
whyWrong.d: Confidentiality within the group does not address whether the requirement may be imposed.

questions.stem: A student has told several friends he intends to die by suicide and has been making bizarre comments in class. Knapp and VandeCreek (2003) indicate that a faculty member questioning him about his mental state would be:

choices.text: unacceptable, since 7.04 bars requiring students to disclose personal information
acceptable only where the program's materials warned of such questioning
acceptable, as necessary to evaluate or obtain assistance for him
unacceptable unless the student first consents to discussing his mental state

questions.explanation: Standard 7.04's second exception covers information necessary to evaluate or obtain assistance for a student whose personal problems may be interfering with education or training, or posing a threat to others. The example given is a student showing signs of depression and suicidal ideation.

whyWrong.a: This states the rule while ignoring the exception that squarely applies.
whyWrong.b: Advance notice in program materials is the *other* exception; either alone suffices.
whyWrong.d: Requiring consent would defeat the purpose of an exception aimed at students in difficulty.

questions.stem: Standard 7.04's second exception permits requiring personal information where it is necessary to evaluate or assist a student whose personal problems may be interfering with training, or:

choices.text: affecting the student's academic standing in the program
causing conflict with other members of the student's cohort
likely to delay the student's expected date of graduation
posing a threat to others

questions.explanation: The exception reaches personal problems that may be interfering with education or training, or that pose a threat to others. Both limbs are stated in the standard.

whyWrong.a: Academic standing is not the trigger; interference with training or threat to others is.
whyWrong.b: Interpersonal conflict alone does not meet the threshold stated.
whyWrong.c: Delayed graduation is not one of the two conditions.

questions.stem: At the end of the training year Dr. Nakamura dismisses an intern for inadequate performance. The intern had never been told what level of performance was expected, nor warned that hers was problematic. Under Standard 7.06 the dismissal is problematic because evaluations must:

choices.text: rest on actual performance against relevant, established program requirements
be conducted by at least two supervisors acting independently of one another
be subject to an appeal process specified in the training agreement
be delayed until the intern has completed a full year of supervised work

questions.explanation: Standard 7.06 requires timely and adequate feedback and evaluations based on actual performance on relevant and established program requirements. The section notes a psychologist would not suddenly dismiss an intern who had received neither a statement of expectations nor prior warning.

whyWrong.b: The standard does not require two independent evaluators.
whyWrong.c: An appeal process is good practice but is not what 7.06 requires.
whyWrong.d: Nothing requires a full year before evaluation; the problem is the absence of expectations and warning.

questions.stem: Standard 7.06 requires that psychologists provide students with feedback that is:

choices.text: written and countersigned by the student
timely and adequate
delivered at the midpoint and end of each training period
reviewed by the program director before being given

questions.explanation: Standard 7.06 requires psychologists to provide students with timely and adequate feedback about their performance, alongside evaluations grounded in actual performance against established requirements.

whyWrong.a: No countersignature requirement appears in the standard.
whyWrong.c: The standard sets no fixed schedule of feedback points.
whyWrong.d: Director review is not required by the standard.

questions.stem: Dr. Ferreira is attracted to a doctoral student in her own department whom she does not currently teach, but who will take her required seminar next year. Under Standard 7.07, a sexual relationship with this student would be:

choices.text: permitted, since she holds no evaluative authority over him at present
permitted if she arranges for a colleague to grade him in the seminar
prohibited, since she is likely to have evaluative authority over him
prohibited only once he has actually enrolled in her seminar

questions.explanation: Standard 7.07 reaches students and supervisees over whom psychologists have, or are likely to have, evaluative authority — and those in their department, agency, or training center. The anticipated authority brings this within the prohibition.

whyWrong.a: This ignores the standard's forward-looking phrase, which covers authority that is likely to arise.
whyWrong.b: Delegating grading does not remove the student from her department or the anticipated authority.
whyWrong.d: Waiting for enrolment misreads a prohibition framed to cover likely future authority.

questions.stem: Standard 7.07 prohibits sexual relationships with students and supervisees who are in the psychologist's department, agency, or training center, or:

choices.text: who have been enrolled in the psychologist's program within the past two years
who are receiving any form of financial support from the institution
whose research the psychologist has agreed to review or examine
over whom the psychologist has or is likely to have evaluative authority

questions.explanation: The standard's second limb reaches anyone over whom psychologists have or are likely to have evaluative authority, which is what makes evaluative authority rather than the label of student the operative element.

whyWrong.a: No two-year look-back appears in the standard.
whyWrong.b: Financial support from the institution is not the criterion.
whyWrong.c: Examining research may create evaluative authority, but the standard states the broader test.

questions.stem: Regarding former students and supervisees, and students in other departments, the prohibition in Standard 7.07:

choices.text: may not apply, since it is framed around current status and evaluative authority
applies with the same force, since the power differential persists indefinitely
applies for a fixed period of two years after the training relationship ends
is replaced by Standard 10.08, which governs relationships with former clients

questions.explanation: The section notes the prohibition clearly applies to a psychologist's current students and supervisees but may not apply to former students and supervisees, or to students in other departments.

whyWrong.b: The standard is framed around current status and evaluative authority rather than a permanent bar.
whyWrong.c: The two-year period belongs to Standard 10.08 on former therapy clients, not to 7.07.
whyWrong.d: 10.08 concerns former therapy clients, a different relationship entirely.

questions.stem: A psychologist with limited experience treating drug addiction is invited to lead a professional workshop on the topic. Accepting would most directly conflict with the requirement that psychologists:

choices.text: identify paid advertisements as such under Standard 5.02
take reasonable steps not to misrepresent their work when teaching
avoid multiple relationships with workshop participants
obtain informed consent from participants before instruction begins

questions.explanation: Standards 7.01 through 7.06 require reasonable steps to ensure psychologists do not misrepresent themselves or their work when teaching, supervising, or designing programs. Leading a workshop on a problem one has limited experience with is the section's example.

whyWrong.a: 5.02 concerns advertising identification, not competence to teach.
whyWrong.d: Informed consent governs services to clients and research participants rather than workshop attendance.

questions.stem: All of the following are accurate statements about Standard 7.04 EXCEPT:

choices.text: it generally prohibits requiring personal disclosure in a course or program
an exception applies where the requirement appears in admissions materials
it bars any inquiry into a student's circumstances without written consent
an exception applies where a student's problems may threaten others

questions.explanation: Standard 7.04 restricts requiring disclosure in a course or program and supplies two exceptions. It does not impose a blanket written-consent requirement on any inquiry into a student's circumstances.

whyWrong.a: This is accurate — it states the general rule.
whyWrong.b: This is accurate — it is the first exception.
whyWrong.d: This is accurate — it is part of the second exception.

questions.stem: A supervisor gives an intern no substantive feedback all year, then rates her as deficient in the final evaluation on criteria never previously mentioned. The clearest problem is that:

choices.text: the evaluation should have been conducted by the training director
the intern was not given the chance to evaluate her supervisor in turn
the supervisor failed to document the supervision sessions adequately
feedback was neither timely nor tied to established requirements

questions.explanation: Standard 7.06 requires timely and adequate feedback and evaluations based on actual performance against relevant, established program requirements. Both elements fail where criteria are introduced only at the end.

whyWrong.a: Who conducts the evaluation is not what 7.06 addresses.
whyWrong.b: Reciprocal evaluation is not a requirement of the standard.
whyWrong.c: Documentation is a record-keeping matter under Standard 6.

questions.stem: A program's brochure states that all applicants must be prepared to discuss personal material in a required experiential course. A student objects after enrolling. Under Standard 7.04, the requirement is:

choices.text: permissible: it was clearly stated in the program's promotional materials
impermissible, since students cannot waive the protection 7.04 provides
permissible only if the student's disclosures are excluded from grading
impermissible unless the student's personal problems threaten others

questions.explanation: The first exception in 7.04 applies where the disclosure requirement is clearly stated in admissions or other promotional materials, so applicants know of it before applying.

whyWrong.b: The standard supplies exceptions rather than an unwaivable protection.
whyWrong.c: Excluding disclosures from grading is not the condition the exception sets.
whyWrong.d: The threat-to-others limb is the second exception; the first suffices on these facts.

questions.stem: Dr. Oyelaran supervises an intern at a community agency and begins a consensual sexual relationship with her. The relationship is:

choices.text: permitted, since the relationship is fully consensual on both sides
prohibited, since she is a supervisee in his agency
permitted if he transfers her supervision to another psychologist first
prohibited only where the agency's own policy forbids such relationships

questions.explanation: Standard 7.07 explicitly prohibits sexual relationships with students or supervisees who are in the psychologist's department, agency, or training center, or over whom the psychologist has or is likely to have evaluative authority.

whyWrong.a: Consent does not remove the prohibition, which exists because of the power differential.
whyWrong.c: She remains in his agency, which the standard covers independently of who supervises her.
whyWrong.d: The Ethics Code applies whatever the agency's internal policy says.

questions.stem: Considering Standards 7.04 and 7.06 together, a training program that requires personal disclosure and then uses what students reveal to evaluate them should at minimum:

choices.text: obtain a signed waiver of confidentiality from every enrolled student
arrange for an external examiner to conduct all student evaluations
state the requirement in program materials and evaluate on set criteria
limit the disclosures to material the student volunteers spontaneously

questions.explanation: 7.04 permits requiring disclosure where the requirement is clearly stated in admissions or promotional materials, and 7.06 requires evaluations to rest on actual performance against relevant, established program requirements. Both conditions bear on this arrangement.

whyWrong.a: A waiver is not the mechanism either standard specifies.
whyWrong.b: External examination is not required by either provision.
whyWrong.d: Confining disclosure to volunteered material would leave the requirement itself unaddressed.

questions.stem: A department chair asks whether Standard 7.07 would reach a relationship between a faculty member and a student in an entirely separate department whom the faculty member will never teach or evaluate. The best answer is that the prohibition:

choices.text: applies, since any faculty-student relationship carries a power differential
applies, since the two are employed by the same institution
does not apply, and no other provision of the Code is relevant
may not apply, though the multiple-relationship standards may still bear on it

questions.explanation: 7.07 is framed around the psychologist's own department, agency, or training center and around evaluative authority held or likely to be held, so it may not reach students in other departments. Standard 3.05 on multiple relationships can still be relevant.

whyWrong.a: The standard is not framed around any faculty-student pairing but around department and evaluative authority.
whyWrong.b: Shared employment is not the test the standard applies.
whyWrong.c: This is right about 7.07 but wrong to conclude no other provision could bear on the situation.
